title: Λέων καὶ βάτραχος
part: The Lion and the Frog (Chambry 201 · Perry 141)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 201 (= Perry 141). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων ἀκούσας βατράχου κεκραγότος ἐπεστράφη πρὸς τὴν φωνήν, οἰόμενος μέγα τι ζῷον εἶναι.
sentences.tr: Leōn akousas batrachou kekragotos epestraphē pros tēn phōnēn, oiomenos mega ti zōion einai.
sentences.l: A lion, having heard a frog croaking, turned towards the sound, thinking it was some large animal.
sentences.n: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the creature heard and a supplementary participle for what it was doing. κεκραγότος is a perfect with present force: κράζω forms its perfect in this way, so 'has set up a cry' simply means 'is crying out'.

sentences.t: Προσμείνας δὲ μικρὸν χρόνον, ὡς ἐθεάσατο αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς λίμνης ἐξελθόντα, προσελθὼν κατεπάτησεν εἰπών· « Εἶτα τηλικοῦτος ὢν τηλικαῦτα βοᾷς ; »
sentences.tr: Prosmeinas de mikron chronon, hōs etheasato auton apo tēs limnēs exelthonta, proselthōn katepatēsen eipōn· « Eita tēlikoutos ōn tēlikauta boāis ; »
sentences.l: And having waited a short time, when he saw him come out of the pond, he went up and trampled him, saying: « So then, being of such a size, do you shout on such a scale? »
sentences.i: He waited a little; and when he saw him come out of the pond, he went up and trod him flat, saying: « So then — no bigger than that, and all that outcry? »
sentences.n: τηλικοῦτος and τηλικαῦτα are the same word twice over, once of the frog's size and once of the size of his shouting; the joke is the repetition, and English has to make the two halves out of different material.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα γλωσσαλγίαν οὐδὲν πλέον τοῦ λαλεῖν δυνάμενον ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra glōssalgian ouden pleon tou lalein dynamenon ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against a man of prattling tongue, able to do nothing more than talk, the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the man who is all tongue and can do nothing beyond talking.
sentences.n: γλωσσαλγία is literally 'tongue-ache' — the chatter of a man whose tongue will not rest. As Chambry prints it the word is a bare accusative noun standing beside ἄνδρα where an adjective would be expected; it is best read as an accusative of respect, 'a man in the matter of prattle', though a corrupted adjective is possible. οὐδὲν πλέον τοῦ λαλεῖν is an articular infinitive after a comparative: nothing more than the talking.
